title: Pronominal Suffixes
subtitle: ־ה ־הא ־הם ־ך ־כם
intro: Arabic doesn't say "his book" with a separate word for "his." It glues a short ending onto the noun: כתאב + ה = כתאבה, "his book." These endings are the single biggest reason a word you know looks unfamiliar — the stem is hiding under a suffix. Learn the handful of endings and the stem jumps back out.

sections.heading: The core endings
sections.body: Each ending stands for a possessor (on a noun) or an object (on a verb or preposition). They are nearly identical to the Hebrew ones you already feel.

examples.note: רבה = his Lord; לה = to him.
להם = to them; מעהם = with them.
רבי = my Lord; ־ני on a verb = me.

sections.heading: On prepositions: tiny but everywhere
sections.body: The most common words on the page are a one-letter preposition plus a suffix. Recognize these and whole sentences open up.

sections.heading: Finding the stem
sections.body: To read a long word, peel the ending off the back and the article off the front. What's left is usually a word you know.

examples.note: יד (hand) + ־ה (his) — the same יד as Hebrew.

quiz.q: What does the ending ־ה mean in רבה?
Peel the suffix: what is the stem of אסמה?
